newsitem.title: USA: US TREASURIES END LOWER AS RETAIL SHUNS 30-YR SALE.
newsitem.headline: US TREASURIES END LOWER AS RETAIL SHUNS 30-YR SALE.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended markedly lower on Thursday, as retail customers shunned the afternoon's 30-year bond auction, forcing dealers to substantially cheapen up the issue late in the session.

In the third and final leg of its quarterly refunding auctions, the Treasury sold $10.0 billion 30-year bonds at an average yield of 6.445 percent and a stop-out rate of 6.452 percent -- pretty much in line with expectations.
Market participants said the auction was the best of the three this week.
The Treasury sold three-year notes on Tuesday and 10-year notes on Wednesday.
The note auctions were deemed sloppy, but the issues traded well afterwards.
Thursday's bond sale was a reversal in that the auction went well, although not spectacular, but the new bonds had tremendous difficulty finding a new home.

"It was an OK auction but I think there had gotten to be a unanimous feeling of bullishness in the marketplace," said a head trader at a large primary dealership. "Everyboy got long; no one set up short and there was little followthrough."
For a brief, shining moment it looked as if the auction and the post-distribution would be a rousing success as the market rallied nearly a half-point.
But that did not last long as retail did not succumb to dealers' hopes of selling the new 30-year bond at the auction price.
As such, the when-issued 30-year bond's yield rose, ending the session at its low of 6.50 percent.
"The customer community is more disciplined than the dealer community," lamented the head trader.

As for the outstanding 30-year bond, it closed at 101-8/32, down 20/32. Its yield jumped to 6.53 percent from 6.48 percent late Wednesday -- the first time the bond closed above a 6.50 percent yield since July 21.

"We are back to fair levels," said Scott Graham, co-head bond trader at Prudential Securities Inc, adding that he expects buying to emerge here. "Retail now gets the chance to buy this stuff cheaper."
Helping the selloff late in the day were stops broken after the September bond contract breached below its 114-16/32 support and as dealers sold long Treasuries for mortgages.
Treasuries opened with a firm tone, which continued into the early part of the morning.
The market shrugged off a 25,000 rise in initial jobless claims to 300,000 in the August 2 week, a five percent gain in July chain store sales and a 1.9 percent rise in June wholesale inventories.

Late in the morning, Treasuries came off its highs -- of about a 1/4-point -- and hovered around unchanged levels heading into the auction. In the afternoon, as the market was heading lower, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City presidnet Thomas Hoenig said the economy was "uniformly very good."
Hoenig cautioned about inflation, and said the Fed was watching labor benefit costs, but he noted the strong dollar has helped to keep inaflation tame.
While not a huge market mover, the remarks were viewed negatively and was just another reason the market ended the day at its lows.
Late in the session, the Fed reported that U.S. consumer installment credit was unchanged in June after rising $2.5 billion in May.
In late trading, the new 10-year note was at 99-6/32. Its yield was at 6.24 percent, up from 6.22 percent.
The five-year note was down 4/32 at 99-14/32 to yield 6.13 percent. The two-year was 1/32 lower at 99-29/32 to yield 5.93 percent.

At the short end of the maturity spectrum, the three-month bill rate was up two basis points at 5.16 percent and the six-month was up three basis points at 5.23 percent. The year bill was unchanged at 5.22 percent.
